docs.title: LinkedIn Archive
docs.text:
Turn LinkedIn data export archives into a searchable database.

linkedin-archive reads the .zip file LinkedIn gives you when you request a copy of your data, or the folder you extracted it to, and loads it into SQLite or PostgreSQL. Import each new export as it arrives: importing the same export again changes nothing, and a newer export adds only what is new.

go install github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/cmd/liarchive@latest

liarchive import Basic_LinkedInDataExport_11-18-2026.zip
liarchive search 'acme (shares OR equity OR "stock options")'

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Full-text search over every message, including the Archive and Spam folders that are easy to miss in LinkedIn's own interface.
  • Repeat imports are safe. Each record remembers the first and latest export it appeared in, so you can see what is new and what has disappeared.
  • Nothing is lost. Messages, connections, conversations, invitations and saved items get their own tables. Every other file in the export is kept row by row.
  • Local and private. The tool makes no network calls. SQLite is the default, so your data stays in one file on your machine.
  • PostgreSQL when you need it, through the same --db flag.
  • Library first. The liarchive command is a thin layer over Go packages you can import into your own programs.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text: If you want to… Read Install the command Installation Get your data from LinkedIn Exporting Your LinkedIn Data Load an export, or a newer one Importing Find a message Searching Messages Use PostgreSQL or change the database file Databases Query the tables with SQL Data Model and SQL Use the Go packages Go Library

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: An export contains personal data about you and the people you have talked to. Keep databases and exports out of version control. The repository's .gitignore already excludes *.db, *.zip and export folders.

docs.title: Data Model and SQL
docs.text: You can query the database directly with SQL, for example with sqlite3 linkedin-archive.db or psql. The examples on this page are SQLite; most work unchanged in PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Table One row per Key columns import_runs Imported export sha256, source_name, export_kind, imported_at, stats persons Person seen anywhere in the archive key, profile_url, name connections First-degree connection first_name, last_name, company, position, email, connected_on, person_id conversations Message thread conversation_id (LinkedIn's ID), title messages Message sent_at, from_name, sender_url, to_names, subject, body_text, content, folder, conversation_id, sender_id message_recipients Message–recipient pair message_id, person_id invitations Connection invitation from_name, to_name, sent_at, direction, message saved_items Saved post or item url, saved_at, title, author, extra raw_records Row of any other export file file, data (JSON)

connections, conversations, messages, invitations, saved_items and raw_records also have first_seen_import_id and last_seen_import_id.

Notes on columns:

  • persons.key is the person's normalized profile URL, or name:<name> when there is no URL.
  • messages.content is the original text, which may be HTML. messages.body_text is the plain-text version used for search.
  • messages.conversation_id and messages.sender_id refer to the id column of conversations and persons. LinkedIn's own conversation ID is conversations.conversation_id.
  • messages.to_names is copied as-is from the export. Use message_recipients for reliable recipients, because names can contain commas.
  • Times are stored in UTC.

docs.title: Who messages you most
docs.text:
SELECT p.name, p.profile_url, count(*) AS messages
FROM messages m
JOIN persons p ON p.id = m.sender_id
GROUP BY p.id
ORDER BY messages DESC
LIMIT 20;

docs.title: Connections by company
docs.text:
SELECT company, count(*) AS people
FROM connections
WHERE company <> ''
GROUP BY company
ORDER BY people DESC
LIMIT 20;

docs.title: Read a whole conversation
docs.text:
Use the conversation: value from a search result:

SELECT m.sent_at, m.from_name, m.body_text
FROM messages m
JOIN conversations c ON c.id = m.conversation_id
WHERE c.conversation_id = '2-YTQ3MjU0ZDkt...'
ORDER BY m.sent_at;

docs.title: Full-text search in SQL (SQLite)
docs.text:
SELECT m.sent_at, m.from_name, snippet(message_fts, 1, '[', ']', '…', 20)
FROM message_fts
JOIN messages m ON m.id = message_fts.rowid
WHERE message_fts MATCH '"tender" AND "offer"'
ORDER BY bm25(message_fts);

docs.title: Read files that don't have their own table
docs.text:
Each row is stored as a JSON object keyed by the CSV header:

SELECT json_extract(data, '$.Name') AS skill
FROM raw_records
WHERE file = 'Skills.csv';

In PostgreSQL, use data ->> 'Name' instead of json_extract.

docs.title: Changes between imports
docs.text:
New since the latest import:

SELECT sent_at, from_name, substr(body_text, 1, 80)
FROM messages
WHERE first_seen_import_id = (SELECT max(id) FROM import_runs)
ORDER BY sent_at;

Connections that were in an earlier export but not the latest:

SELECT first_name, last_name, company
FROM connections
WHERE last_seen_import_id < (SELECT max(id) FROM import_runs);

docs.title: Import statistics
docs.text:
import_runs.stats holds the per-file counts shown when you import:

SELECT id, source_name, json_extract(stats, '$.messages.inserted') AS new_messages
FROM import_runs;

docs.title: Databases
docs.text: linkedin-archive stores data in SQLite by default and can use PostgreSQL instead. The tables are the same in both. They are defined once with Ent and created or updated automatically when the tool opens the database.

docs.title: Choose the database
docs.text:
Every command accepts --db. You can also set the LIARCHIVE_DB environment variable. The flag wins if both are set.

liarchive --db sqlite:$HOME/data/linkedin.db stats

export LIARCHIVE_DB=sqlite:$HOME/data/linkedin.db
liarchive stats

If neither is set, the database is linkedin-archive.db in the current directory.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text:
Form Meaning sqlite:linkedin.db File relative to the current directory sqlite:///home/me/linkedin.db Absolute path sqlite::memory: In-memory database that disappears on exit (useful for tests)

SQLite is the best choice for personal use:

  • The whole archive is one file you can copy, back up or delete.
  • No server to run.
  • No C compiler needed. The driver is pure Go and includes full-text search.

The database uses write-ahead logging, so you may see -wal and -shm files next to it while it is open.

docs.title: PostgreSQL
docs.text:
liarchive --db 'postgres://user:password@localhost:5432/linkedin?sslmode=disable' import export.zip

Both postgres:// and postgresql:// work. Create the database first; the tables and the search index are created on first use.

Consider PostgreSQL when:

  • The archive feeds a shared or hosted service.
  • You want to join it with data that already lives in PostgreSQL.
  • Several people's archives share one database. In that case you will want access controls such as row-level security, which you need to set up yourself.

Keep credentials out of shell history

Set LIARCHIVE_DB in your environment instead of typing a password on the command line.

docs.title: Moving between databases
docs.text: There is no built-in copy between SQLite and PostgreSQL. Import the original export files into the new database instead. Imports produce the same records and keys, so the result matches.

docs.title: Exporting Your LinkedIn Data
docs.text: linkedin-archive works only from LinkedIn's official data export. It does not log in to LinkedIn or collect data from the website.

docs.title: Request an export
docs.text:
1. On LinkedIn, open Settings & Privacy.
  2. Go to Data privacy → Get a copy of your data.
  3. Choose what to download (see below) and select Request archive.
  4. LinkedIn emails you when the file is ready. Download the .zip.

You can import the .zip directly. There is no need to extract it first, though an extracted folder works too.

docs.title: Basic and Complete exports
docs.text:
LinkedIn offers two kinds of export.

Basic Complete Typical wait About 10 minutes Up to 24 hours Messages, connections, invitations Yes Yes Profile, positions, skills, endorsements Yes Yes Your posts, comments and reactions No Yes Saved items (saved posts) No Yes

liarchive accepts either one and detects which kind it is. The kind is shown when you import and by liarchive imports.

Saved posts

Saved items appear only in a Complete export. You can also request just that category of data, which usually arrives much sooner than a full Complete export.

docs.title: What is in an export
docs.text:
An export is a set of CSV files. The ones linkedin-archive turns into tables are:

File Table messages.csv, and other *_messages.csv files such as learning_coach_messages.csv messages, conversations, persons Connections.csv connections, persons Invitations.csv invitations Saved items or saved posts files saved_items Every other CSV file raw_records (each row kept as JSON)

docs.title: Known quirks
docs.text:
The importer handles these for you. They are listed here so the results make sense.

  • Each export is a full snapshot. It contains your whole history, not just what changed since the last one.
  • Messages have no ID. The importer builds a stable one from each message's conversation, time, sender and content.
  • Some senders have no profile URL. Sponsored InMail and "LinkedIn Member" messages are matched by sender name instead.
  • Message text is often HTML. The original is kept, and a plain-text copy is used for search.
  • Connections from deactivated accounts appear with only a connection date. They are counted as skipped because there is nothing to identify them by.
  • Dates come in many formats, such as 2026-11-17 20:18:55 UTC, 31 Oct 2026 and 10/30/26, 5:04 PM. Times without a time zone are treated as UTC.

docs.title: Import an export
docs.text:
liarchive import Basic_LinkedInDataExport_11-18-2026.zip

The output shows what was found in each file:

Basic_LinkedInDataExport_11-18-2026.zip: import #1 (basic export) in 837ms
  ENTITY                   SEEN  NEW   SKIPPED
  connections              2911  2911  34
  conversations            1430  1430  0
  invitations              310   310   0
  messages                 4809  4809  0
  raw:Skills.csv           58    58    0
  ...
Column Meaning SEEN Rows read from this export NEW Rows not in the database before SKIPPED Rows with nothing to identify them by, such as connections from deactivated accounts

Rows named raw:<file> come from files that don't have their own table. They are stored in raw_records so nothing is lost.

You can import several exports at once, oldest first:

liarchive import exports/2025-06.zip exports/2026-11.zip

docs.title: Import again, or import a newer export
docs.text:
Imports are safe to repeat.

  • The same export again is recognized by its content hash and skipped:

    Basic_LinkedInDataExport_11-18-2026.zip: already imported (import #1)

  • A newer export adds only records that weren't there before. Records already in the database are matched and updated, not duplicated.

Each record stores two import numbers:

Field Meaning first_seen_import_id The import where the record first appeared last_seen_import_id The most recent import that still contained it

So after importing a newer export you can ask what is new and what has gone, for example a connection who is no longer in your list. See Data Model and SQL.

A message that moved folders between exports, for example from Inbox to Archive, keeps its identity and has its folder updated.

Basic after Complete

Only files present in an export update "last seen". Importing a Basic export after a Complete one does not make your posts or saved items look removed.

docs.title: List imports
docs.text:
liarchive imports

ID  IMPORTED                   KIND   SOURCE                                    NEW MESSAGES  NEW CONNECTIONS
1   2026-11-19T07:12:03-08:00  basic  Basic_LinkedInDataExport_11-18-2026.zip  4809          2911

docs.title: Count rows
docs.text:
liarchive stats

imports        1
people         3426
connections    2911
conversations  1430
messages       4809
invitations    310
saved_items    0
raw_records    2556

docs.title: Saved items
docs.text:
liarchive saved
liarchive saved --json

This lists saved posts and items with their URL and the date you saved them. They come only from a Complete export. See Exporting Your LinkedIn Data.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Go 1.26 or later.
  • No C compiler is needed. SQLite support uses a pure-Go driver.

docs.title: Install the command
docs.text:
go install github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/cmd/liarchive@latest

To install a specific release:

go install github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/cmd/liarchive@v0.1.0

Check that it works:

liarchive --help

docs.title: Use as a library
docs.text:
go get github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive

See Go Library for the packages and an example.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive
cd linkedin-archive
go build ./cmd/liarchive

docs.title: Commands at a glance
docs.text:
Command What it does liarchive import <zip or dir>... Import one or more exports liarchive search [query] Full-text search messages liarchive imports List the exports you have imported liarchive stats Show how many rows each table holds liarchive saved List saved items (Complete exports only)

Every command accepts --db to choose the database. See Databases.

docs.title: Go Library
docs.text:
The liarchive command is a thin layer over packages you can use directly.

go get github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive

docs.title: Packages
docs.text: Package Purpose archive Open an export (zip or folder); read CSV files by header name; typed records store Open SQLite or PostgreSQL by DSN and create or update the tables importer Import an archive into a store search Query and result types, and the query syntax parser search/engine Pick the right search implementation for a store search/sqlitefts, search/pgfts SQLite and PostgreSQL search implementations ent Ent client and schema, for your own queries

docs.title: Import and search
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"

    "github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/archive"
    "github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/importer"
    "github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/search"
    "github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/search/engine"
    "github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/store"
)

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()

    s, err := store.Open(ctx, "sqlite:linkedin.db")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer s.Close()

    a, err := archive.Open("Basic_LinkedInDataExport_11-18-2026.zip")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer a.Close()

    res, err := importer.Import(ctx, s.Client, a)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("import #%d, %d new messages\n", res.ImportID, res.Stats["messages"].Inserted)

    srch, err := engine.New(ctx, s)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    results, err := srch.Search(ctx, search.Query{
        Text:   `acme (shares OR equity)`,
        Folder: "ARCHIVE",
        Limit:  10,
    })
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    for _, r := range results {
        fmt.Println(r.SentAt, r.From, r.Snippet)
    }
}

docs.title: Read an export without a database
docs.text:
The archive package works on its own, for example to convert an export to another format:

a, err := archive.Open("export.zip")
if err != nil {
    return err
}
defer a.Close()

msgs, err := a.Messages()        // []archive.Message
conns, err := a.Connections()    // []archive.Connection
invs, err := a.Invitations()     // []archive.Invitation
saved, err := a.SavedItems()     // []archive.SavedItem

// Any file, as rows keyed by header name
t, err := a.ReadCSV(a.Find("Skills.csv"))
for _, row := range t.Rows {
    fmt.Println(row.Get("Name"))
}

archive.New accepts any fs.FS, such as fstest.MapFS in tests.

Helpers:

Function Purpose archive.ParseTime(s) Parse any date format found in exports archive.HTMLToText(s) Strip HTML and collapse whitespace archive.NormalizeProfileURL(u) Normalize a LinkedIn profile URL

docs.title: Query with Ent
docs.text:
store.Store.Client is a regular Ent client:

import "github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/ent/connection"

conns, err := s.Client.Connection.Query().
    Where(connection.CompanyContains("Acme")).
    All(ctx)

docs.title: Parse search queries
docs.text:
search.Parse turns the query syntax into terms, if you want to build your own search on top:

terms, err := search.Parse(`acme (shares OR "stock options") -recruiter`)

It returns search.ErrOnlyNegated, search.ErrUnbalanced or search.ErrNestingTooDeep for queries it can't use.

docs.title: Searching Messages
docs.text:
liarchive search runs a full-text search over the subject, text and sender name of every message, in every folder.

liarchive search 'tender offer'

2026-10-01 09:00  Tender Desk  [INBOX]  https://www.linkedin.com/in/tender-desk
  A [tender] [offer] for Example Corp shares is open.
  conversation: 2-YTQ3MjU0ZDkt...

1 result(s)

Matching words are shown in [brackets]. Results are sorted by how well they match.

docs.title: Query syntax
docs.text:
Syntax Meaning Example a b Both words stock options a OR b Either word shares OR equity "a b" Exact phrase "secondary sale" -a Exclude a word ipo -recruiter pre* Words starting with pre invest* (a OR b) c Grouping acme (shares OR equity)

Rules to keep in mind:

  • AND binds tighter than OR. a b OR c means (a AND b) OR c. Use parentheses when you mean a AND (b OR c).
  • OR must be in capitals. A lowercase or is searched as a word.
  • An excluded word applies to the group it is in. (a OR b) -c finds messages with a or b that don't mention c.
  • A query can't consist only of excluded words.
  • Searches ignore case. SQLite also ignores accents, so resume matches résumé; PostgreSQL does not.

Word stemming

English words are reduced to their root, so shares also matches share, shared and sharing. This finds more variations, but can also match words used in a different sense. Narrow the results with more words, a phrase, or an excluded word.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Filters can be combined with a query, or used on their own to list messages.

Flag Meaning --from <text> Sender name or profile URL contains this text --folder <name> Only this folder: INBOX, ARCHIVE or SPAM (any case) --since YYYY-MM-DD Sent on or after this date --until YYYY-MM-DD Sent before this date -n, --limit <n> At most this many results (default 50)

Without a query, results are sorted newest first.

# Everything one person sent you
liarchive search --from "Jane Doe"

# Archived messages from 2025 that mention a phrase
liarchive search '"stock options"' --folder archive --since 2025-01-01 --until 2026-01-01

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Flag Output (none) Readable list with a snippet around the matching words --full The full plain text of each message instead of a snippet --json JSON, for scripts and other tools 
liarchive search 'shares OR equity' --json | jq '.[] | {sentAt, from, folder}'

Each JSON result includes messageId, key, conversationId, conversationTitle, sentAt, from, senderUrl, to, folder, subject, snippet and rank.

docs.title: Example: finding an offer you half-remember
docs.text:
Say you recall someone offering to buy, or lend against, your shares in a private company, but not who or when:

liarchive search 'acme (shares OR equity OR stock OR liquidity OR secondary OR tender OR investor*)'

Then narrow down:

# Drop recruiting messages that mention equity
liarchive search 'acme (shares OR equity) -hiring -role -recruit*'

# Read the full text of the best matches
liarchive search 'acme liquidity' --full -n 5

To read the whole conversation for a result, use its conversation ID with SQL. See Data Model and SQL.

docs.title: How search works
docs.text:
Database Engine SQLite FTS5 index with English stemming, kept up to date automatically as messages are imported PostgreSQL Built-in full-text search with the english configuration and a GIN index

The index is created the first time you import or search. Both databases accept the same query syntax.

docs.title: Release Notes v0.1.0
docs.text: Release Date: 2026-11-19

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This is the first release of linkedin-archive, a Go library and command-line tool that turns LinkedIn data export archives into a searchable SQLite or PostgreSQL database.

Import the .zip LinkedIn gives you, search every message in every folder, and import newer exports as they arrive without creating duplicates.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text: go install github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive/cmd/liarchive@v0.1.0

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
go get github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive@v0.1.0

Requires Go 1.26 or later. No C compiler is needed.

docs.title: Import exports directly
docs.text:
• Reads the export .zip directly, or an extracted folder.
  • Accepts both Basic and Complete exports and detects which one it is.
  • Reads CSV files by header name rather than column position, so minor LinkedIn format changes don't break imports.
  • Handles the export's quirks: the notes block at the top of Connections.csv, byte-order marks, repeated column names, HTML message bodies and many different date formats.

docs.title: Safe repeat imports
docs.text:
• The same export imported twice is detected by content hash and skipped.
  • A newer export adds only new records. Existing records are matched, not duplicated.
  • Each record stores the first and latest import it appeared in, so you can see what is new and what is gone between exports.
  • Messages that moved folders between exports, for example Inbox to Archive, are updated in place.

docs.title: Full-text message search
docs.text:
• Searches subject, text and sender name across Inbox, Archive and Spam.
  • Query syntax: words, "phrases", OR, -exclude, prefix* and (groups), the same on both databases.
  • English stemming, so shares also matches share.
  • Filters by sender, folder and date range, with text or JSON output.
  • SQLite uses an FTS5 index kept up to date automatically. PostgreSQL uses built-in full-text search with a GIN index, with every search term passed as a query parameter.

docs.title: Nothing is lost
docs.text: Messages, conversations, people, connections, invitations and saved items get their own tables. Every other CSV file in the export is kept row by row in raw_records as JSON.

docs.title: SQLite or PostgreSQL
docs.text:
• SQLite by default, using a pure-Go driver: one local file, no server.
  • PostgreSQL through the same --db flag or the LIARCHIVE_DB environment variable.
  • Tables are defined with Ent and created automatically.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Description liarchive import <zip or dir>... Import one or more exports liarchive search [query] Full-text search messages liarchive imports List imported exports liarchive stats Row counts per table liarchive saved List saved items

docs.title: Go packages
docs.text: Package Purpose archive Read exports and parse typed records store Open SQLite or PostgreSQL by DSN and migrate importer Repeat-safe import search, search/engine, search/sqlitefts, search/pgfts Message search ent Ent schema and generated client

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Saved items are mapped by header name. The column names have not yet been confirmed against a real Complete export; columns that aren't recognized are kept in saved_items.extra.
  • Posts, comments and reactions from Complete exports are stored only as raw records for now.
  • PostgreSQL is covered by an end-to-end test that runs only when LIARCHIVE_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN names a test database.
  • Times without a time zone, such as invitation dates, are treated as UTC.
  • Connections from deactivated accounts, which have only a date, are counted as skipped and not stored.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: See the roadmap. Phase 2 covers confirming the saved-item columns against a Complete export, tables for posts, comments and reactions, endorsements and positions, and a report of changes between imports.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text: Build Phase 1 end to end against SQLite first, keeping engine-specific code in search/sqlitefts and search/pgfts so the Ent model stays portable. Add saved items early (Phase 2, RMI-LIARCHIVE-006) because the column mapping is header-driven and tolerant, then confirm it against a real Complete export.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Module setup. go.mod for github.com/grokify/linkedin-archive, dependencies at verified latest versions: entgo.io/ent, github.com/spf13/cobra, modernc.org/sqlite, github.com/jackc/pgx/v5.
  2. archive package. Open(path) (*Archive, error) returning an fs.FS-backed archive; ReadCSV(name) returning header-keyed rows; ParseTime; typed readers Messages(), Connections(), Invitations(), SavedItems(), and Files() for raw iteration.
  3. Ent schema. Entities listed in the TRD; generate with go generate ./ent.
  4. store package. Open(ctx, dsn) (*Store, error) returning the Ent client, the *sql.DB, and the dialect; runs client.Schema.Create.
  5. importer package. Import(ctx, client, archive) (*Result, error) implementing the semantics in the TRD.
  6. search packages. Query parser, FTS5 translation, Postgres implementation, and engine.New(ctx, store) choosing by dialect.
  7. CLI. Cobra commands over the library.
  8. Tests. Synthetic fstest.MapFS exports; in-memory SQLite.
  9. Docs. README with install, export instructions and examples.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation LinkedIn changes file or column names Header-driven parsing; raw-record fallback preserves unknown data Saved-item columns differ from the assumed headers Unmapped columns kept in extra; RMI-LIARCHIVE-007 validates against a real export Messages have no stable ID Content-hash key with occurrence index Timestamps without a zone (invitations) Treated as UTC and documented Personal data committed by accident .gitignore covers *.db, *.zip and export directories; tests are synthetic

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: linkedin-archive turns LinkedIn data export archives (the .zip produced by Settings → Data privacy → Get a copy of your data) into a searchable, queryable database. Users import each new export as it arrives; the database accumulates history across exports without duplicating records.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
LinkedIn's export is a zip of loosely structured CSV files. It is difficult to answer simple questions with it:

  • "Which messages mentioned X, and who sent them?"
  • "When did I connect with this person, and what did we last discuss?"
  • "Which posts did I save, and when?"

The web UI's message search is limited, conversations that were archived or filtered to spam are easy to miss, and each export is a full snapshot that cannot be diffed against earlier ones by hand.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
• Individual professionals who want to search their own LinkedIn history locally and privately.
  • Developers who want an importable Go library for parsing LinkedIn exports into structured records.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Import a LinkedIn export .zip (or an extracted directory) with one command, without manual extraction or cleanup.
  2. Re-importing the same export is a no-op; importing a newer export adds only new records and updates "last seen" tracking on existing ones.
  3. Full-text search over messages across all folders (inbox, archive, spam), with filters for sender, folder and date range.
  4. Structured access to connections, invitations and saved items.
  5. Never lose data: files the importer does not model are preserved as raw rows.
  6. Run locally on a single file database by default (SQLite); optionally run against PostgreSQL for hosted or shared deployments.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Scraping LinkedIn or calling LinkedIn APIs. The only input is the official export.
  • Fetching the content of saved posts or shared URLs from LinkedIn.
  • Multi-tenant hosting in the first release.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text: ID Use case UC-1 Find a half-remembered inbound message, such as an offer to buy or finance private-company equity, by searching for terms across every folder. UC-2 List all messages from or to a person, in conversation order. UC-3 Import a newer export and see what was added since the previous import. UC-4 List saved posts/items with their URLs and saved dates. UC-5 Look up a connection's company, position and connection date.

docs.title: Data availability
docs.text:
LinkedIn offers two export types:

  • Basic (fast, ~10 minutes): profile, connections, messages, invitations, endorsements, positions and similar.
  • Complete (up to 24 hours): Basic plus activity such as Shares.csv (your posts), Comments.csv, Reactions.csv and saved items.

Saved items are therefore only available from the Complete export, or from a targeted request for that category. The importer must accept either export type and must not assume any file is present.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
• All processing is local; the tool makes no network calls.
  • The repository contains no real export data. Tests use synthetic fixtures.
  • Database files are excluded from version control by default.

docs.title: Success metrics
docs.text:
• A Basic export of ~5,000 messages imports in under 10 seconds on a laptop.
  • Search returns results in under 200 ms for that dataset.
  • Importing the same archive twice yields zero new rows.

docs.title: Roadmap: linkedin-archive
docs.text: Phase status is derived from the status of its RMIs.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Library-first: all logic lives in importable packages; the CLI is a thin adapter.

cmd/liarchive        Cobra CLI (import, search, stats, imports, saved)
archive/             Read export zip/dir; header-driven CSV parsing; typed records
ent/schema/          Ent schemas (source of truth for tables)
ent/                 Generated Ent code
store/               Open database by DSN (sqlite / postgres), run migrations
importer/            Idempotent import service
search/              Searcher interface and query syntax
search/sqlitefts/    SQLite FTS5 implementation
search/pgfts/        PostgreSQL full-text implementation

docs.title: Database support
docs.text:
Engine Driver Use SQLite modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go, FTS5 built in) Default, local single file PostgreSQL github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib Hosted or shared deployments

Ent defines all tables and runs migrations for both engines. Full-text search is engine-specific and lives in separate packages behind the search.Searcher interface:

  • SQLite: an FTS5 external-content table message_fts over messages(subject, body_text, from_name) with the porter unicode61 tokenizer (stemming, diacritics folded). Insert/update/delete triggers keep it in sync; it is built from existing rows when first created.
  • PostgreSQL: a GIN expression index on to_tsvector('english', subject || ' ' || body_text || ' ' || from_name). Queries combine plainto_tsquery, phraseto_tsquery and prefix to_tsquery values with &&, || and !!, binding every user term as a parameter.

DSN format:

  • sqlite:///path/to/file.db or sqlite:file.db
  • postgres://user:pass@host/db?sslmode=disable

docs.title: Input handling
docs.text:
• Input is a .zip file or an extracted directory; both are read through fs.FS, so no extraction step is needed.
  • CSV files are parsed by header name, not column position. Missing columns yield empty values; extra columns are kept.
  • Preamble lines before the header (e.g. Connections.csv starts with a Notes: block) are skipped by locating the first line containing the expected header fields.
  • A UTF-8 BOM is stripped.
  • Duplicate header names (e.g. Ad_Targeting.csv) are suffixed (_2, _3).
  • File names are matched case-insensitively by base name, so files in subdirectories and minor naming changes are tolerated.

docs.title: Date parsing
docs.text:
Exports use many formats. A shared parser tries, in order:

Example Source 2026-11-17 20:18:55 UTC messages 2025/10/08 11:50:14 UTC endorsements 2026-04-26 14:07 UTC learning 31 Oct 2026 connections 10/30/26, 5:04 PM invitations, saved jobs (no zone; treated as UTC) Wed Nov 18 20:32:07 GMT 2026 company follows Jul 2023 positions RFC 3339 fallback

N/A and empty strings parse to "no value".

docs.title: Data model (Ent)
docs.text:
All imported entities carry first_seen_import_id and last_seen_import_id fields to support snapshot diffing. (The import entity is named ImportRun because import is a Go keyword.)

Entity Natural key Notes ImportRun sha256 of the archive bytes (zip) or sorted file hashes (dir) source_name, export_kind (basic/complete/unknown), imported_at, files (JSON) Person key = normalized profile URL, else name:<lowercased name> profile_url, name Connection person first_name, last_name, email, company, position, connected_on Conversation LinkedIn CONVERSATION ID title, source_file Message key = SHA-256 of (conversation id, date, sender url, from, subject, content) plus an occurrence index for exact repeats within one export sent_at, from_name, to_names, recipient_urls, subject, content (raw), body_text (HTML stripped), folder, attachments, source_file; edges: conversation, sender, recipients Invitation SHA-256 of row from_name, to_name, sent_at, message, direction, inviter_url, invitee_url SavedItem SHA-256 of (url, saved at) url, saved_at, title, author, content, extra (JSON for other columns) RawRecord (file, row_hash) data (JSON map of header → value) for files not modeled above

docs.title: Message parsing details
docs.text:
• Message files: messages.csv plus any *_messages.csv with the same header (e.g. learning_coach_messages.csv); source_file records which.
  • Recipients come from RECIPIENT PROFILE URLS (comma separated). The TO name list cannot be split reliably because names can contain commas, so it is stored verbatim.
  • Senders without a profile URL (sponsored InMail, "LinkedIn Member") are keyed by name.
  • body_text strips HTML tags, unescapes entities and collapses whitespace.

docs.title: Saved items
docs.text: The importer recognizes any file whose base name matches saved*item* or saved*post* (case-insensitive). It maps URL-like and date-like columns by header name (Saved Item, Url, Link, Saved At, Saved Date, Created Time, …) and keeps all other columns in extra. Column names are confirmed against a Complete export before release.

docs.title: Import semantics
docs.text:
1. Hash the input. If an ImportRun with that hash exists, report "already imported" and stop.
  2. Create the ImportRun row.
  3. In one transaction per file, upsert each record by natural key:
  4. New: insert with first_seen = last_seen = this import.
  5. Existing: update last_seen (and mutable fields such as folder).
  6. Only files present in this export update last_seen, so a Basic export does not mark Complete-only records as removed.
  7. Rebuild the search index.
  8. Store per-entity counts (seen, inserted, skipped) on the ImportRun. Rows with no usable identity (deactivated connections with no name or URL) are counted as skipped. Identical raw rows are kept distinct by occurrence index.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
search.Query:

Field Meaning Text Query string From Sender name or profile URL substring Folder INBOX, ARCHIVE, SPAM, … (empty = all) Since, Until Date range Limit Max results (default 50)

Query syntax (portable across engines): bare words are ANDed, "quoted phrases", OR, -excluded, prefix* and (groups). AND binds tighter than OR, and excluded terms apply to the group they appear in. Both engines stem English words, so shares also matches share and sharing.

Results include the message, conversation id/title, sender, a highlighted snippet and a rank.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
liarchive import <zip|dir>        [--db DSN]
liarchive search <query>          [--from --folder --since --until --limit --json]
liarchive imports                 list imports with counts
liarchive stats                   row counts per entity
liarchive saved                   list saved items

--db defaults to $LIARCHIVE_DB, else sqlite:linkedin-archive.db.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Unit tests for CSV parsing, date parsing, HTML stripping, query translation and key generation.
  • Importer tests against an in-memory SQLite database using a synthetic export built in the test (fstest.MapFS).
  • PostgreSQL tests run only when LIARCHIVE_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN is set.
